Teachers and Support Staff, Payroll—Minister’s Statements
1. TRACEY MARTIN (NZ First)  to the Minister responsible for Novopay: Does
he stand by his statement of 11 February 2014, “education payroll is the most complex
in New Zealand and more work remains to be done to simplify the business processes to
ensure it runs as smoothly as possible each year”?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Minister
responsible for Novopay : Yes, the ministerial inquiry  found that the school payroll
system is hugely complex, pa rticularly for end-of-year and start-of-year pays. For
instance, at the start of the year 80 percent of all staff on the payroll have adjustments to
their pay. There are currently around 80 se parate allowances for teachers and 99
allowances for principals. Th at is 99 different allowanc es applying to different
principals under several different collectiv e agreements, and those can change at any
time, depending, for instance, on the number of  staff who are employed in the school.
Teachers who have changes made at the start of the year may have had their allowances
expire, they might be on fixed-term contract s, or they might be on contracts that go
from one term to the next. All of these ha ve to be restarted at the beginning of each
year, and it is not surprising that there is the odd error when 80 percent of all teachers
have changes to the payroll at the start of the year.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can he confirm that the educati on payroll is no mo re complex than
when it was under the previous payroll providers Multi Serve and Datacom?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is likely, but under those systems there were
considerable errors. In fact, for many re asons, it would be a good idea to simplify the
payment of teachers so, for instance, there are not 99 separate allowances payable to
school principals. I think a lo t of teachers and a lot of th e people responsible for data
entry in the schools would like to see a simpler way of paying teachers so that there are
no errors.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Is he aware that under Novopa y, many teachers cannot match a
single payslip from the last 15 months to deposits in their bank accounts and are unable
to identify the cause of the problem in order to rectify it; if so, what confidence can he
have in the error reports that he is currently receiving?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Crown and the Minister of Education must meet their
obligations to pay teachers. There is no choice about that. If teachers believe they have
not been paid the right amount, then there is  now a fairly comprehensive process set up
to ensure they are paid correctly, because that is a legal obligation of the Crown. I
would say, though, that it will  be less expensive for th e Crown, more certain for
teachers, and certainly less costly for the payr oll system if we could negotiate collective
agreements that are significantly less comple x than the ones that currently apply. Large
amounts of resource were spen t under the previous admini strative system correcting
continuous errors in pay.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can he confirm that the 2013 payr oll error reports are now overdue
to schools and that as many of the 2012 repor ts themselves were incorrect, they now
require double-checking by schools?
16320 Questions for Oral Answer 5 Mar 2014

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot confirm that. What I can confirm though is that the
complexity of the payroll, which was previ ously buried in an expensive system run by
Datacom, is now obvious to every school. In the long run all our interests will be better
served by negotiating a collective agreement th at does not have 99 different changeable
allowances for school principals.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did he state last year when he  became Minister responsible for

items.speaker: Novopay
items.text: “I want to see within three months the situation where, as much as possible,
workloads for administrators are back to wher e they were before this thing started,”; if
so, is he satisfied that he has delivered on that promise?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. The error rates on this massive, complex payroll are
now well under 1 percent, and the Minister is satisfied that he has delivered on
undertakings. It can be improved now only by making the underlying collective
agreements less complicated than they are.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Is he aware of a school in Rodn ey that has lost $29,000 out of its
operations grant following the failure of Novopay’s debt collection arm to collect
overpayments from support staff, some of whom were non - New Zealanders and have
subsequently left the country?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not aware of that particular case, but the Minister is
certainly aware of the problem of overpaym ents and debt collection, and considerable
effort has been applied to try to resolv e that on behalf of schools. Again, the pay
arrangements for teachers are more complicated than for almost anyone except the
police. In both cases we would get bett er results for everybody with much less
complicated collective agreements.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can we take from his answers th at the National Party believes in
flexibility inside of education for everybody apart from teachers and their payroll?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. The Government believes it needs to meet its legal
obligations to pay people who work hard, who educate our children, and who contribute
much to New Zealand’s economic and social  development, and we will do everything
we can to meet those obligati ons—in fact, more than what we can; we actually have to
meet the obligations. I am simply making the point that in the longer run teachers would
be better off, the Government would be bette r off, and the system would be much less
expensive if we could simplify the arrangement s. There is simply no justification for 99
separate allowances for school principals. That is nuts and we should try to change it.
Prime Minister—Statements
2. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by his statement that “the true builders of that future are the millions of
New Zealanders working in the homes, the businesses, the industries of our country”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I stand by that statement. But, just to
be technically correct, the member should not e that the statement was from the Speech
from the Throne that was actually deliver ed by the Governor-General in December

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What is the Prime Minister doing to protect our sawmilling
industry as 400 sawmill workers’ jobs are curren tly on the line at Southern Cross Forest
Products in South Otago because it has gone into receivership?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am just not briefed on that particular situation, but what I
would say is that the Government has been working very hard, actually, to make sure
the economy is efficient, productive, and workin g well, and that all of those factors are
in play, which is why our economy is the e nvy of so many othe r countries around the
world.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Since the Prime Minister—
5 Mar 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 16321

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Supplementary question, the Hon David Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Since the Prime Minister did not notice those 400 jobs that
were in danger, what about the 120 worker s who lost their forestry jobs at the
Tachikawa Forest Products sawmill in Roto rua months ago, or the more than 10
workers who lost their lives in the industry in the last 13 months?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is good news that the me mber is focusing on people who
might lose their jobs. In any one given—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The level of interjection coming for this answer is now
completely—[Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister sh ould not start that way, but
when he was given a question that starte d the way it did, then the Opposition could
expect the sort of answer the Prime Minister is giving.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can you elaborate on what
you found offensive about that question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I did not find anything offensive. Otherwise I would have ruled it
out of order. But if you recall the wording of  the Hon David Cunliffe, he said words to
the effect “Since the Prime Minister does not know of that incident”, and then led into
his question. They were—[ Interruption] Order! They were unnece ssary to the question
and, because they were given in the question, they invite a very wide response from the
Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The labour markets in New Zealand are very dynamic and in
any sort of 3 month period around about  100,000 jobs are created and somewhere
between 100,000 and 200,000 jobs in any similar period can be lost. But what we do
know is that the economy is growing, 1,500 people a week are leaving welfare for work,
the economy is showing—and the unemployment rate is falling. It is one of the reasons
that consumer and business confidence is rising, but there will  always be some
companies that shed employees for a variety of different reasons, and we know that one
of those companies could be an organisation called the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Were the 52,000 New Zealanders who have left for Australia
since he took office helped by the fact that this Government presided over the closing of
the Hutt and Hillside engineering workshops  after KiwiRail awarded contracts to
offshore manufacturers rather than to New Zealand producers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: For a start off, it is pleasing to see that we are now on a record
10-year low of New Zealanders leaving for Australia. It is equally true that if we look at
the unemployment rate in New Zealand, it is  currently 6 percent and the participation
rate is far higher than Australia’s—although its official rate is 6 percent, if it had the
same participation rate, in fact its unemploy ment rate would be ove r 10 percent. I am
surprised that the member is actually raisi ng these individual items without getting to
his feet to talk about the many, many thous ands of New Zealanders who are gaining
jobs each week.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Since the Prime Minister  is now making up future
unemployment rates, would he like to make  up some asbestos regulations so that
imported Chinese locomotives do not poison New Zealand railway workers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I said to the member yester day, that is in breach of the
contract. I have seen a report today that says that there are no harmful effects, but that is
a matter for KiwiRail, ultimately, to do things . But what I would be  interested in doing
is not—not, I say—making up the two names of people who gave David Cunliffe
money. I would be interested in finding out  exactly who they are. Why does not the
member tell us? If it is Kim Dotcom, why does he not just say it is him?

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order. It will be heard in silence.
16322 Questions for Oral Answer 5 Mar 2014

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: The Prime Minister is establishing himself as a fantasist in the
public’s mind, but that—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can the member please resu me his seat. I have invited the
member to raise his point of order. I have told the House that this point of order will be
heard in silence. The member needs to now raise the point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: The question is one of rele vancy and whether the Prime
Minister’s conjecture has anything to do w ith the question of asbestos regulation.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not need assistance from the Prime Minister. The
difficulty the member has is the way he asked his question. He led into the start of his
question by saying “Since the Prime Minister is making it up …”. If the member wants
a clear, concise answer, as I told him yesterday, he needs to ask a clear and concise
question. [Interruption] I have addressed the matter.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What is the Prime Minister doing to ensure that specialist
industries such as rail, c onstruction, and boatbuilding have any future under his
Government when KiwiRail gives contr acts overseas and ferries are built in
Bangladesh, not in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There has been a very broad range of initiatives undertaken by
the Government through the Business Growth Agenda, and what we know is that they
are working. If you look at the BNZ-Bu siness New Zealand Performance of
Manufacturing Index, which is the best reflection of ma nufacturing, we know that
month after month after month—I think for the last 14 or 15 months in a row—we have
seen an increase in manufacturing output in  New Zealand. What we also know is that
from time to time New Zealand companies w ill bid on a contract that they will not get
because someone will be able to provide it at  a much cheaper rate. On the advice that I
saw in relation to the ferry that the member actually aske d the question about, it was
multiples more expensive if it was built in New Zealand. So if the member is telling us
and telling New Zealand taxpayers that the wa y that he would run the show is to spend
enormous amounts of money buying only New Z ealand products, that is interesting on
two fronts.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What about the tax on the jobs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I tell you what, let me ju st finish this point, because you
might find it quite interesting. The first point would be that taxpayers would be paying a
lot more. The second point the member is  making is that New Zealand companies
should buy only New Zealand products, but when  Australian supermarkets wanted to
buy only Australian products, that member went nuts.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Can the Prime Minister unders tand why the unemployment
rate has now climbed to 9.3 percent in the Bay of Plenty, and what steps is he taking to
assist the kiwifruit industry and those work ers who are bearing th e personal tragedy of
the Psa disease in terms of lost jobs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Two things. Firstly, the mo ment Psa was discovered, the
Government put in, I think off the top of  my head, $25 million, which was matched by
the industry. We worked very hard to make sure that the kiwifruit growers were back on
their feet. I have met with qui te a number of them and the industry over th e years. My
understanding is that they are doing a lot bette r, but obviously it has been a very tough
time. But one thing I will say is that we take about 8,000 people a year on the
Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, which wo rks heavily in the horticulture sector,
including, obviously, kiwifruit. My understand ing is that that sector is lobbying the
Minister very aggressively for an increas e because it is so busy it cannot get enough
staff.
5 Mar 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 16323
State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Progress of Share Offer
3. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance: What
progress is the Government making with its share offer programme, which is freeing up
money for reinvestment in new public assets  without having to increase Government
debt?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Last week the Government
confirmed that the last of its share offers for a minority shareholding in Genesis Energy
will proceed later this month. The offer is expected to open in the second half of March,
with the company likely to be listed on the market around mid-April. All of this, of
course, is subject to market conditions. We will set out the details for the float over the
next few weeks. As with the other share offe rs, New Zealanders will  be at the front of
the queue, and we remain committed to at least 85 percent Kiwi ownership. The
Genesis Energy share offer will be structured  to meet the Government’s objectives of
achieving good value for taxpayers as well as  providing opportunities for New Zealand
investors.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What were some of the Governme nt’s objectives for the share offer
programme, and have those objectives been met?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the objectives was to enable the Government to
finance new infrastructure with the savings of New Zealanders rather than by borrowing
from foreign banks. There were also a number of other objectives. We wanted to help to
deepen the capital markets so that as New Zealand goes into a growth phase, more New
Zealand businesses can go to the public market to raise the capital they need in order to
invest in New Zealanders’ skills and higher incomes in the future. It has also enabled us
to free up money for reinvesting in priority  public assets like schools, hospitals, and
ultra-fast broadband. So far we have raised around $4 billion to do that, and that is $4
billion of New Zealanders’ savings rather than $4 billion of borrowing from foreign
banks.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What are some of the features of  the Genesis share offer that will
help build interest among New Zealand investors?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is obviously up to investors to decide what level of interest
they take in the share offer, but the Gove rnment will introduce new features to the
Genesis offer. First, the shar es will be priced at the st art of the offer period, which
means that Kiwi investors know the price when they apply for shares. Secondly, we
have expanded the range of what we expect to  sel l to  3 0  to  4 9  percent of the shares,
subject to market conditions. The Government wants to be able to test demand in the
market before making a final decision. We will also be offering a loyalty bonus scheme
and a more succinct investment statement for retail investors.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Without the share offer programme , what alternative approaches
could the Government have taken to pay for new public assets such as schools and
hospitals?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There are other ways of financ ing it, for instance, increasing
taxes or introducing new ones, such as th e dopey internet tax the Labour Party is
proposing. Another option would be not to invest in these public assets and to tell New
Zealanders to make do with what they ha ve. We did not do that. We could have gone
out and borrowed $4 billion from foreign bankers, whom the Opposition would rather
we do business with, but we chose to go to  New Zealand savers. Finally, there is
another option. We could have set up a trust and asked for secret donations!
Pike River Mine Disaster—Release of Information
4. ANDREW LITTLE (Labour)  to the Attorney-General: Will he release all
correspondence between the Christchurch Cr own Solicitor or any other solicitor acting
16324 Questions for Oral Answer 5 Mar 2014
for the Ministry of Business, Innovati on and Employment, and counsel for Peter
Whittall on the decision not to proceed w ith the prosecution of Mr Whittall under the
Health and Safety in Employment Act 1992 relating to conditions at the Pike River
Mine that lead to the deaths of 29 miners; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: No, because that is not
a decision for me to make.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of that answer and in lig ht of the public statement made by
counsel for Peter Whittall on Friday, 28 February at 4.23 p.m. that “Neither Mr Whittall
nor Mr Grieve have any issue with any of  their letters on this matter being made
public.”, and thereby waiving their legal pr ofessional privilege, why will he not now
ensure that that correspondence is released?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The member did not listen, or did not listen
carefully, to my answer to his first questi on. That is not a decision for me to make.
Perhaps I can help the honourable member by referring him to th e Solicitor-General’s
Prosecution Guidelines  and the introduction to it by  me, which says “Under our
constitutional arrangements, the Attorney-General is responsible through Parliament”—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: This is humble.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Well, instead of making unpleasant
comments, Mr Robertson should listen, because, I am sure Mr Little would agree, this is
a very serious matter.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! If the Minister  could just give his answer, it would be
helpful.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I will go back for a minute, because Mr
Little at least is taking this seriousl y. Under our constitutional arrangements, the
Attorney-General is responsib le through Parliament  to the citizens of New Zealand for
prosecutions carried out by or  on behalf of the Crown. In practice, however, the
prosecution process is superintended by the Solicitor-General who, pursuant to section
9A of the Constitution Act 1986, shares all the relevant powers vested in the Office of
the Attorney-General.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What information about the state or progress of the prosecution did
Cabinet have before it when deciding not to ta ke action to ask the shareholders in Pike
River, including Crown enti ties, to make good the repa ration orders made by the
District Court on 5 July 2013?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Regrettably, the member did not listen to the
first answer to the question. Ca binet did not make a decision,  and the implication in his
question is deeply constitutionally offensive.  These are decisions that are made by the
Solicitor-General. Cabinet has no place in de ciding on the initiation, the continuance, or
the bringing to an end of a prosecution.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Was the offer on behalf of Mr Whittall, to pay $3.41 million to the
families of the dead miners, taken into acc ount in the decision not to proceed with the
prosecution and in the subsequent decision to  offer no evidence and seek a discharge,
the equivalent of an acquittal?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: As I said, these are matters for the Solicitor-
General. To the best of my knowledge, when  the Solicitor-General and, through him,
the Crown prosecutor in Christchurch were determining the matter, that was a factor
that was taken into account. But there were a number of matters that meant that the
Crown decided not to proceed with the prosecution.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How was the public interest test , required under paragraph 5.1.2 of
the Solicitor-General’s prosecution guidelines of 1 July 2013, met in this case, in light
of the clear findings of the royal commission of inquiry of the level of negligence by the
5 Mar 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 16325
mine owner’s officers, leading up to the fatal explosion on 19 November 2010 and the
fact that 29 men died at work in one fell swoop, causing widespread public alarm?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Once again, I have to bring the member back
to the prosecution guidelines and to the pe rson who makes the decision, and the factors
that are taken into account in making the de cision. These matters are free from political
interference, or at least in a National Government they are.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can I invite you to go
back and look at that answer, look at the Cabinet Manual , and look at the Standing
Orders, and inform us who is answerable in Parliament for those decisions if it is not the
Attorney-General.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will accept the invitation from the member, and I will certainly
have another look at it.
Southern District Health Board—Dispute with South Link Health
5. KEVIN HAGUE (Green)  to the Minister of Health : When were Ministry of
Health officials first informed that the di spute between the Southe rn District Health
Board and South Link Health involved allega tions of the misuse of public funding, and
when were they first informed that this alleged misuse was suspected to involve
elements that could be fraud?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I am advised that this complex
commercial dispute is over savings from pharmaceutical and laboratory contracts from
1995 to 2002, and it has been ongoing for over a decade. I am advised that the Ministry
of Health has been aware, over all of this tim e, that Southern District Health Board has
had concerns over the agreed and proper use of savings, and that is why there is a
dispute. In relation to the s econd part of his question, I am  advised that they became
aware of concerns about fraud in late 2013. The member knows that this matter is now
with forensic accountants to see whether ther e is an issue of fraud, but the member may
also be interested to know that the Ministry of Health has advised me that it has seen no
evidence that suggests fraud.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does the Minister continue to maintain that he did not know that there
were allegations of misuse of funds prior to  late 2013, as he answer ed in this House in
the last sitting session, when this fact had been extensively covered by mainstream and
specialist health sector media for more than a decade?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Yes, I do, because, as I said to the member last week, we have
searched our records, the ministry’s records, and the records of the district health board
and we have found no evidence in respect of that 2010 advice that  he talked about.
Look, the member can cast as many aspersions as he likes on whatev er individuals he
wants to look at, but the fact is that the fo rensic accountants are now looking at this. It
will be interesting to see what they come up with, but I have received advice from the
Ministry of Health that they have seen no evidence that suggests fraud.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker . It is unclear from the Minister’s
answer whether he is answer ing yes or no to th is basic question of whether he is
continuing to maintain—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I can assist the member. I heard the Minister say that, yes, he
maintains his position.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does the Minister continue to maintain that he did not know that there
were allegations of misuse of funds prior to late 2013, when his written answers today
show that his own office was communicating directly with the district health board chief
executive on multiple occasions about this very issue in 2010?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: That is because at the time they were seeking to get mediation
and arbitration. There had been no advice  given to me that there was any fraud
16326 Questions for Oral Answer 5 Mar 2014
associated with that. The member has got to acknowledge that this has been going on
for 12 years. It is a very complex situation—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question related to
allegations of the misuse of funds, not about fraud specifically—that is a separate matter
and a subset. The Minister has been claimi ng that he had no knowledge prior to late
2013 that there were allegations of the misuse  of funds. It would be  good if his answer
could address that point.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am going to invite the member to repeat his question because the
Minister had started his answer  before he was interrupted by the point of order. Repeat
the question please.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does the Minister continue to maintain that he did not know that there
were allegations of the misuse of funds pr ior to late 2013, when his written answers
today show that his own office was communicat ing directly with the district health
board chief executive about this very issue on multiple occasions in 2010?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think the member is trying to create some sort of mystery
around this use of the words “m isuse of funds”. As I said in my main question, the
whole issue—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The main question?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: —answer—of this debate over  the last 12 years has been
whether there has been agreed and proper us e of the money. If you want to call that
“misuse of funds”, the member can, but all of his questions have been about the issue of
fraud. The reason why we are talking about this—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.  The Minister is effectively trying
to litigate the question, rather than answer it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No. The Minister has a ddressed the question. The member
himself referred to the issue of the misuse  of funds. The Minister has addressed the
question. If the member has further searchi ng supplementary questions, that is the way
that he might get the sort of answer that he is after.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Given that the Minister does conti nue to maintain that he did not
know that there were allegati ons of misuse of public funds  prior to late 2013, has he

Tertiary Education and Skills Training—Tertiary Education Strategy 2014-19
6. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills
and Employment : What announcements has the Government made on the Tertiary
Education Strategy for New Zealand?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Earlier today I launch ed in Auckland the Tertiary Education Strategy
2014-19, which sets out the Government’s exp ectations and directi on of the tertiary
education sector for the next 5 years. The future tertiary system needs to be more
outward facing and engaged in order to re spond to the international expansion of
tertiary education, the needs of a growing economy, and new technologies. That means
having strong links to industry, communit y, schools, and the global economy. The
Tertiary Education Strategy is designed to he lp guide tertiary educ ation investment and
the actions needed from the Government, tertiary education organisations, business, and
the wider community to significantly improve further our tertiary education outcomes.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What are the priorities for tertia ry education identified in the
Tertiary Education Strategy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The strategy identifies six key priorities: delivering skills
for industry, getting at-risk young people in to a career, boosting achievement for M āori
and Pasifika, growing education linkages, strengthening research-based institutions, and
improving adult literacy and numeracy. Good progress has already been made in many
of these areas. Since 2008 there has been a ri se in the number of full-time students, we
are seeing more graduates than ever before and at higher levels, and we had 10,000 new
apprentices sign up between March and Dece mber of last year. The number of M āori
students enrolled in qualifications at Bach elor’s level or higher has increased from
17,500 in 2007 to nearly 29,000 in 2012. The number of Pasifika students enrolled in
qualifications at Bachelor’s  level or higher has rise n from 8,500 in 2007 to nearly
5 Mar 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 16329
12,000 in 2012. Our tertiary sector must cont inue to adapt and change in order to
provide the skills and qualifications that New Zealanders need in or der to contribute in
the labour market in innovative and competitive ways.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How is the Government strengthening research-based institutions?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Alongside the Tertiary Education Strategy I launched
today, I also announced changes to simplif y and strengthen the structure of the
Performance-based Research Fund. The Performance-based Research Fund rewards and
encourages excellent tertiary education research by assessing quality, allocating funding
based on results, and publishing informa tion on performance. The changes I have
announced today are designed to simplify the re search assessment process to save time
and reduce costs for organisations and rese arch staff; reward tertiary education
organisations to attract external research income from international sources or New
Zealand industry or not-for-profit organisa tions or iwi; strengthen public reporting on
research performance; and reward tertiary educ ation organisations that recruit, develop,
and retain new researchers. We have a system with a number of strengths when
compared with other funding systems around the world. These changes will build on
those strengths, reduce complexity, and lower compliance costs.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora t ātou. How can the Minister
stand by his Tertiary Education Strategy, which provides for M āori achievement and
success, when his Tertiary Education Commission is shutting down the only M āori
national centre of research excellence, Ngā Pae o te Māramatanga?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member raises a very fair point. The centres of
research excellence review is going on at th e moment, and the research society of New
Zealand is actually doing the work to evalua te those centres of re search excellence and
determine which should be funded from the end of 2015 onwards. My understanding is
that the member notes that that particular centre of research excellence is not, at this
stage, proposed for funding. It will be up to th e institutions as to how they run them. It
is important that this is an independent process with scientists measuring the progress of
each of these centres of research excellen ce and that they are not being assessed by
politicians sitting in this Chamber.

improved technology and better connectivity?

involvement in the management of their faci lities. It would not come as a surprise. We
generally do not have armies of Govern ment builders—although we might if Labour
and the Greens got in—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The question has been answered at the
start.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Will she rule out allowing international companies to run or
manage parts of the New Zealand public school system through a public-private
partnership?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and I would not see why the Associate Minister would.
The whole purpose of this is to try to reduce the cost and deliver savings over traditional
procurement by the ministry. It is rumoured to be between 2 percent and 8 percent. We
will know that through the proc ess. That allows us extra money to spend on the actual
education. If the member is saying that it is more important not to have certain types of
companies involved than to get a good school f acility built and to have more money for
education, well, good on her.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: How many other schools have been identified for possible
selection as potential public-private partnerships, as suggested in the Cabinet paper
released yesterday, and does th at mean she will consider existing schools and buildings
for private management?
5 Mar 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 16335

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not aware of any specif ic cases in that respect,
although I am not sure that it would be a shoc k, horror, or probe to  suggest that we are
always looking at ways in which we can improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the
management of school facilities, which is very  expensive, and we w ould prefer to have
more money to spend on education than on the maintenance of buildings. If we find
better ways of doing that, I cannot see there is a problem with it.
Child Health—Nutrition and Exercise Programmes
11. PAUL FOSTER-BELL (National) to the Minister of Health: What investment
is the Government making in improving nutrition and exercise for pre-schoolers?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Thousands of Waikato preschoolers are
now benefiting from a healthy nutrition a nd activity programme, Under 5 Energize,
developed with $1.1 million of Governme nt anti-obesity funding. Around a hundred
early childhood centres in th e Waikato are now involved w ith the Under 5 Energize
programme, which supports healthy eating and the deve lopment of fundamental
movement skills for children. It is part of a wider programme investing in maternal and
newborn nutrition as recommended by Sir Peter Gluckman.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What changes have centres involved with the Under 5 Energize
project made?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Last week I visited Fairfiel d Kindergarten in Hamilton with
David Bennett and Tim Macindoe, which has been involved with Under 5 Energize, and
there has been a marked difference in the t ypes of food coming in  with the kids. The
staff were also able to identify that their children felt restricted  by bad weather when
wanting to play outside, so the kindergart en has now purchased wet-weather gear so
that the kids are able to play outside in bad weather. They are also bringing fruit to
kindy to share and drinking water is encourag ed. It is a very good effort—I am looking
forward to the evaluation—and another investment under this National-led Government.
Prisoners—Drug and Alcohol Rehabilitation
12. JOANNE HAYES (National)  to the Minister of Corrections : What steps has
the Government taken to improve access to alcohol and drug treatment for prisoners?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am very pleased to advise the
House that there has been a rise of almo st 1,500 percent in places on drug and alcohol
treatment programmes since 2008 for prisoners in public prisons. This financial year
over 3,700 prisoners will have acce ss to treatment for their a ddictions, rising to 4,700
next year. This compares with just 234 prisoners having access to that same treatment in
the final year of the previous Labour-led Government. This Government has expanded
the number of specialist drug treatment units  in prisons from six to nine and has
significantly increased the capacity of these units. In addition, we have also introduced
new brief and intermediary programmes in a ll prisons to ensure those prisoners who
need treatment for their drug addiction receive it.

items.speaker: Joanne Hayes
items.text: Why is the Government focuse d on increasing alcohol and drug
treatment in prisons?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Alcohol and drug addiction is a major driver of crime. Over
half of all prisoners have addiction problems when they enter prison. If we can get them
off the drugs and give them some job skills  and education to find work on release, we
reduce the risk of them going on to commit further crimes. That is why this Government
is focused on increasing the drug and alcohol treatment in our prisons as part of our plan
to reduce reoffending by 25 percent. This work  is delivering results, with a reduction in
reoffending of nearly 12 percent since 2011, meaning nearly 8,700 fewer victims.
16336 Questions for Oral Answer 5 Mar 2014

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . What a week for David Cunliffe. What a week for the
Artful Dodger over there, the Leader of the Opposition. Let us see where he started the
week. He started the week with poll numbers that, frankly, made the David Shearer days
look like the golden age of Labour. If he thought that was a ba d starting point, it was all
going to go from bad to worse for “Tricky” David Cunliffe.
The question on everyone’s lips this week, the question that everyone is trying to get
their heads around, is who is David Cunliffe ? Who is he? Which of the many faces of
David Cunliffe should we believe? Is it the “Politics of Envy” Leader of the Opposition,
who tried to tell New Zealand that he lived  a very middle-of-the-road, middle existence
in his little doer-upper in the s uburbs, when, of course, it turn s out that he is one of the
very wealthy in New Zealand and lives in a mansion in wh at can only be described as
one of the most exclusive suburbs? Is it “Mr Doublespeak”, who promises to the unions
that they can expect that they are on th eir way back to the good old days of the 1970s,
or is it the guy who turns up in front of the businesses and the boardrooms and promises
that all will be all right under the free mark et Harvard graduate going back to Milton
Friedman?
No, I do not think it is any of those. Perhaps it is “Devious Dave”, who came out
with his child payment policy and promised New Zealand that it would apply to nearly
60,000 families, and then had to quietly corre ct it to say: “Oh, when I said 60,000, I
actually meant more like 30,000. But it is all in the numbers—just a small error.”
Interestingly enough, he tried to  blame staff for that one as  well, but he had to accept
responsibility for that. Perh aps it is “Dodgy Dave”, who Ne w Zealand is now learning
funnelled his donations through a secr et trust. Is that not inte resting? This is the same
David Cunliffe who was part of the Labour Government that reformed the electoral
finance laws in relation to donations and railed about transparency and honesty and
accountability. But when it was his turn, what was the advice he took? It was: “Let us
have a secret trust so we don’t have to tell the public who is really backing us.” Is that
not interesting?
You have got Shane Jones, who is quite pr epared to be open with the public. Even
Grant Robertson did not mind telling the public  who was behind him. So what is it with
David Cunliffe? Why is it that he could not be straight w ith New Zealand and tell them
who was funding him? You have to wonder. Now he has come out and when a bit of
pressure comes on he is prepared to name three of the donors. He was quite happy to
take the money of the other two, quite a s ubstantial amount, thousands and thousands of
dollars—he was happy to take it—b ut now that the heat  is on, he would rather just give
it all back and make it go aw ay. Well, I think New Zealan d wants to know who they
were. Who were they? Maybe it was Kim Dotcom. Maybe it was his union mates. How
will we know? This doyen of transparency a nd reform of electoral finance law is now
suddenly “Shady Dave”—“Shady Dave”, who does not want to tell us anything. You
have to say that since Davi d Cunliffe became leader of the Labour Party, it has been
gaffes galore. It has been one shipwreck after another.
That is only the start of them. Who reme mbers his electoral law breach during the
by-election, when David Cunliffe broke the electoral laws, breached the rules and said
“Oh, sorry, it was an error.”? We are hearing a lot of excuses. I think we have heard “It
was an error.”, “It was a mistake of judgment.”, and “In hindsight it was a bad call.” We
have heard “technical glitch”, we have hear d “oversight”, and we have heard “That was
my staff. I didn’t know it wa s happening.” Just this week he managed to throw one of
his own MPs under the bus when he let them take the rap for his own office’s disclosure
5 Mar 2014 General Debate 16337
of draft policy to us. His own office disclo sed the draft policy, and he was quite happy
to throw one of his MPs under the bus. So we can add another one: he is also “Disloyal
Dave”. He is “Disloyal Dave” as well as everything else.
He came out, of course, after the Grammy s and congratulated Lorde. He could not
spell her name right, withdrew the congratulat ions, and blamed it on an error. He could
not get his CV right. That was a mistake, all of that padding and stuff that he had
forgotten he had not actually done. He copied Grant Robertson’s candidacy
announcement—another glitch. He misled the public on Shane Jones’ stance in the
leadership contest. I think the thing is this. What New Zealand knows is that if you
cannot run a party and you cannot run your ow n affairs, you sure cannot run a country.
We do not want any part of “Tricky Dave”.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: The Green Party in Government will put
children at the heart of every decision that we  make, at the heart of all of our policies,
and at the heart of all our work. What did we discover last week? The Government has
been masking, hiding, the number of children who are living in seve re poverty in this
country. It missed out on 20,000 kids last year—20,000 children and their families were
ignored by this Government. The Green Part y will not ignore those children. We will
work to bring them out of the poverty that they suffer. Let us just have a think about the
legacy of John Key. John Key, since he ha s been Prime Minister, has seen 45,000 more
children living in poverty than before he came to power. There are 45,000 more children
and their families in poverty under John Key. The Green Party will change that if we get
a chance to be at the heart of a progressive Government after this 2014 election.
This Government is failing New Zealand’s ch ildren, and it does not need to be that
way. We can make a difference for each of the 285,000 children in poverty. We can
change the lives of each of those children a nd their families. This is how we can do it.
The Green Party will put children and their needs at the heart of all our decisions. We
have already come up with three major sets of  solutions to help address the poverty that
our kids are suffering. Step one is to bring a bout a living wage for families, to raise the
minimum wage, and to make sure that wo rking families have enough money to get by
on. Not only will we do that; we will raise be nefits, because we know that most of the
kids who live in poverty are from benefit- dependent households, and that is because
benefits are too low. Given that work does not solve poverty, actually, under this current
Government, we must also raise the minimu m wage, move to a living wage, and make
sure that benefits are decent enough for families to live on.
We will make sure every family has access to a warm and dry home for their kids
through our Home for Life programme for progr essive ownership, so that ownership of
their own home really is with in the grasp of young families. We will make sure there is
a warrant of fitness for all rental properties—not just a few, like this Government has
done, but all rental properties. We know that  most of the children who live in poverty
live in cold, damp homes. There will be se curity of tenure so those who are the most
vulnerable in their housing, including State house tenants, know they will be able to live
in a home, rent that home, and have some security for themselves and their families
when times get hard.
Finally, there will be school community hubs. Schools are at the heart of their
communities, and we can make sure they can support their communities and their kids
better by relieving teachers and principals of the social obligations, if you like, and the
social difficulties that families face. We w ill have a full-time facilitator in every low-
decile school, a dedicated school nurse, a free school lunch fund for those schools, and
free after-school care for those families. We know that so many kids miss out on
extending their education because their fam ilies cannot afford after-school care and
programmes.
16338 General Debate 5 Mar 2014
We will build 20 new community-based chil dhood education centres, not private but
not-for-profit, on school grounds. I have ta lked about this before. I know a young
woman really well who has two kids—one at  preschool, one at school—with no money
and no car. When she has no food, where can she get help? Well, she will be able to get
help at the school. She will know that he r younger child can go  to early childhood
education there and that her ol der child will get a great public education at that public
school. It is close by, so she can walk to it . The children will be fed through a national
lunch fund that the Green Party will put in place when we are in Government. We can
make a difference for every single one of those children who live in poverty. We will
make that difference when we are part of a progressive Government after this election in
2014. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.role: Minist er for Building and Construction
items.text: In
the last week or so we have been watchi ng the unfolding of a Shakespearean piece of
work on the other side of this House. I am still unable to work out whether it is a
tragedy, a drama, a thriller, a comedy, or a documentary, or all rolled into one. It all
centres on the leader of the Labour Party.
The good news about having been in this House for a long time is that you actually
get to a point where you think you cannot see anything ne w under the sun. But there is
something new, and I want the Labour Party members to listen up. It goes like this. I
have never seen ever, in the history of the New Zealand Parliament, a political leader of
a party who was not voted to that position by his own team. I have never seen that—I
have never seen it. In fact, I do not know of any country around the world that has a
political leader of a party who did not enjoy a majority. So, Mr Cunliffe, I suggest to the
House, starts from behind the eight ball. That is what you would say in the old
vernacular. He starts from behind the eight ba ll, where less than one-third of his team
actually wanted him.
One of the things he could do is win suppor t. He could get out there and have some
real big hits. Can Labour score some hits ? Yes, it can. Shane Jones has shown that.
Shane Jones has shown how to have a really big hit. He has done it. Oh, and guess
what? He did not brief his leader on it and did not discuss it with his leader. Wow! That
is team playing for you, Mr Jones—that is team playing for you.
But Mr Cunliffe’s tragedy cum drama cu m thriller cum comedy keeps unfolding. In
any other sport, be it baseball , softball, or whatever, even in some of the legal things
with regard to offending, we all know of a thing called “three strikes and you’re out”—
“three strikes and you’re out”. No wonder Mr Cunliffe did not support the “three strikes
and you’re out” policy, because I was actuall y going to get up to give this speech,
saying that he has had his three strikes.  There was “baby bonus - gate”. We all
remember “baby bonus - gate”, where he ba dly screwed up the a nnouncement of that.
Then there was “leafy suburb - gate”. We all remember “leafy suburb - gate”. He is an
ordinary common man of the people, and then it turns out that he is earning in the top
0.1 percent of 1 percent of income earners a nd lives in a house worth more than most of
us put together. That was fine. But then we  got “trust-gate”. “Trust-gate” I thought was
a real clincher.
But there are some more. I have had someth ing handed to me just today. Poor Clare
Curran has been blamed—has been blamed—f or the leak of the information and
communications technology policy yesterday. It was her fault—that is what we were all
going to say. It was her fault.  Poor Clare Curran. But I have  just been told that David
Cunliffe’s chief press secretary, Simon Cunliffe—a relation, I presume—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: That’s a bit low.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: What is wrong? Did you hear that? “Chippy”
over there says that it is a bit low to say that  he is a relation. Is he that bad now that you
5 Mar 2014 General Debate 16339
do not want to even claim th at you are a relative of the guy ? How bad is that, when he
does not want to even say he is a relation of his? That is bad.
Let us go to “trust-gate”. What was “trust-gate” about? It was about getting money
into the coffers for your le adership challenge and not telling anybody where it came
from—and not telling anybody where it came from. Well, we have got some speculation
on this side. We think it was Kim Dotcom. We think there is almost no doubt, but we do
not know, you see. They go “Oh, no, no.”, but  we do not know. We do not know where
that money came from. It could be from Kim Dotcom. It could be from Owen Glenn—it
could be from Owen Glenn.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Putin.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, no. My friend up there got carried away and
said it was Putin, but that is not right. It could be Matt McCarten. There is a really good
one. The Unite union got him into power b ecause the caucus did not want him. The
caucus did not want him. They still do not want him. They want him out.
I want to tell that Labour Pa rty that you have go t to be very careful when you are on
the slippery slope. One of the bits of history that I remember was 1990. In 1990
Labour’s then leader, its then Prime Minister , Geoffrey Palmer, just was not cutting the
mustard. I used to talk to Labour backbenche rs and they used to say: “Jeez, I don’t
know what we’re going to do here.” Well, do you know what the Labour Party did? Six
weeks before the general election it said: “W e can’t go on with him.” and it cut him. It
went to Mike Moore and do you know what? Th e old adage of “Cheer  up; things could
be worse.”—well, they cheered up and, sure  enough, things got worse. Labour went out
on a slippery sliding hiding to nothing.
This leader is gone. He is dog tucker. He has had his three stri kes and he should get
out.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Sunday was Children’s
Day. To celebrate the day we went out and as ked Kiwis just what their dreams were for
Kiwi kids. The responses were not something to celebrate. The responses were, in turn,
heartbreaking and infuriati ng. It was a hard lesson in just how tough it is for New
Zealanders and their families, and just how tough life has become for so many under
this Government. It is like this response from Eleanor, a te acher who claims that kids
fall asleep in class because their house is so cold that it keeps them awake. Or the
response from another Kiwi who dreams of a day when “I take my kid to the
supermarket and he wants a lollipop or chocolate, and I can get it for him because I have
got enough money and a good job. I want to see him happy and not crying because I
can’t afford it.” Those are New Zealanders’ dreams for their children under National’s
New Zealand—to be able to afford a lollipop when they take them to the supermarket.
This response is from Angela, who wants kids simply to have clean waterways, green
grass and parks, to enjoy the Kiwi lifestyle. Another pers on dared to dream of a New
Zealand in which kids could “have their pa rents around, not working all hours just to
make ends meet.” It is like the woman in  Papakura, whom I met a few weeks ago, who
works 16 hours to support two teenage boys and who has not had a pay rise since Helen
Clark was the Prime Minister. She is on less than $14 an hour. Shame, shame, shame!
Or this from Byron, who wrote: “I have night mares about being able to afford my son’s
education, and pray that I will be able to help build the finance.”
Then there are the endless, endless dreams of warm houses, of kids not going hungry,
and of parents with decent jobs: “I want to be loved, fed, and secure. I want my kids to
have their basic needs met. I want a family th at I can feed and rais e. I want breakfast,
lunch, and dinner; warm clot hes to wear; a full tummy; a warm, dry home; nourishing
food; warm, clean clothing; and parents who have time. I just want to be valued.” That
is where National is taking New Zealand—to a point where making our kids warm and
16340 General Debate 5 Mar 2014
fed and safe is not a policy, it is a dream. Even more damning is the fact that under
National so many of those dreams will continue to be unfulfilled as the gap between the
haves and the have-nots gets wider and wider.
Let us not forget that in the last fo rtnight we found out that another 20,000 New
Zealand kids are living in poverty because the Government got its numbers wrong, and
that it knew about it before it declared it to this Pa rliament. There are now 285,000
children living below the poverty line, growing up in poverty—more than the
populations of Dunedin and Hamilton combine d. It is a disgrace that so many children
and their families are in poverty and left dr eaming of meeting the basic needs of life
because this Government has washed its hands of them.
Well, Labour has not walked away. We have a dream that we will make a reality. It
is one that we share with Cu rtis and many other kids who have written to us. We stand
for kids being able to follow their dream s, no matter where they  are or how much
money is in their parents’ wallets. Both th e Prime Minister and I had those kinds of
opportunities, but the difference is that hi s Government is pulling the ladder up after
itself while we are extending it for all New Zealanders. That is why we will be
extending the number of jobs out there and making sure New Zealanders in all our
regions have the opportunity for better j obs and higher wages. That is why we
introduced the Best Start package for children.
I note that National is yet to  attack the substance—I wonde r why. It is yet to attack
the substance because either it would like to do it or it does not want to be seen arguing
against the principle of feeding our kids. Giving $60 a week to the families that wrote in
here will make a difference—so will paid parental leave, so will early childhood
education, and so will decent care for the mothers. We want a future for all New
Zealand’s children, not just for some.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: In the months ahead the New Zealand
public get to see two teams lining up toe to toe. They will see the A-Team, clearly led
by a very strong, confident, optimistic, pos itive Prime Minister , John Key. We are
delivering for hard-working New Zealanders every day a stronger economy, more jobs,
higher wages, safer streets and communities, higher levels of achievement in education,
and, of course, better access to health care. And then we have the B-Team—or should
we say the C-Team? Actually, that is probably a bit generous. I think it is the D-Team—
D for David. Or is it “Tricky David”? Or is it “Clumsy Cunliffe”? Or is it “Which-way-
is-up Day” today? Because New Zealande rs right now—actually, do not even worry
about New Zealanders, because the members of his own caucus do not know which way
he is heading. They do not know what he stands for and therefore they do not know
what they stand for.
In terms of talking about standing, it is really  interesting to see that we have seats in
Timaru—for example, the seat of Rangitata . Only a few months ago David Shearer was
saying that Labour was clearly going to retake the provincia l seat of Rangitata. Well,
actually, you cannot even get a candidate, so in terms of trying to get members on your
team, you are obviously struggling—so good luck with that. At the end of the day they
have to be able to hold the ball and not drop the ball, and not drop it more than twice in
one day.
It is really interesting if you talk to and listen to constituents on the street.
[Interruption] Do not mind me, Mr Robertson—just ha ve a little tête-à-tête across the
House. Hard-working New Zealanders have got  things that they are interested in
hearing about. One of them is jobs. We talk a lot in the House about jobs and I want to
talk about some of the things that this G overnment is doing in provincial New Zealand.
Dream on—actually, we should add to David Cun liffe’s title “Dream Chaser”, or today
5 Mar 2014 General Debate 16341
it was the “Chief Fantasy Officer”, in terms of  some of the things that he is dreaming
up.
In hard-working rural and provincial New Zealand, in a seat like Taup ō, what counts
is jobs and the things that th is Government is doing to create  jobs. It is attracting major
international events and keeping them in provincial New Zealand, like the Ironman New
Zealand competition, which celebrated its 30 th anniversary, through the Major Events
Development Fund, which supports these sorts of activities. There has been an $8
million extension to the Cycleway Fund, which helps to maintain significant
infrastructure in pl aces like Tokoroa, P ūtāruru, and T īrau, where jobs are created as a
result of the Waikato River Trail. The fact is that there are tourists and visitors who
come into that area who have never come before. If you look at the new, soon-to-be-
opened Great Lake Trail in Taupō—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: How many jobs?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How many jobs do you get from an Ironman?

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: —that is another thing that brings visitors into our towns and
creates jobs. You are asking about jobs. The number of jobs that came from people who
were previously unemployed in the south Waikato who got jobs because of the Waikato
River Trail is a record that I am proud of. I am proud of people who come off
unemployment benefits and go into work. That is what this Government is doing, and it
is delivering on it every day.
Just last week I was in the electorate with Minister Paula Bennett and we were in one
of the local Work and Income offices talking about one of the challe nges that they are
hearing. Do you know what that challenge is? It is that or ganisations are saying that
they do not have the same number of volunt eers they once had because some of the
people who were volunteering before now have jobs. They have got jobs they need to
turn up to. So I think that is a good problem th at we have as a count ry. There is silence
from the other side now because they do not lik e the fact that we are talking about jobs
and that we are talking about getting people off benefits and into work. Whatever job it
is, we think that it is important. This side of the House values work. We think it is
important that we are getting people off benefits and into work. I, for one, am proud.
Next month at the velodrome, the home of cycling—in Cambridge, not in Hamilton,
as was reported by one of the daily newspapers—we will welcome the Duke and
Duchess of Cambridge. Not only is it for high-performance sport, which this
Government is funding, a large number of the people who will use that  facility are the
community members who are learning to ride. It backs up another initiative that this
hard-working Government is delivering, instead of the dreamers on the other side.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: There is a reason that the
Cabinet Manual has strict rules in place about the decl aration of conflicts of interest. It
is because New Zealand taxpayers expect th at when Ministers go about their business,
particularly when they go overseas, they will do so in a way that is fair, that is good
value for money, and that will not in any way advantage them or anyone they know. It
is my view, and I believe it would be the view of most New Zeal anders, that Judith
Collins taking a trip paid for by the taxpayer to the Shanghai office of a company in
which her husband is one of only three direct ors, going to that office, having her
photograph taken, and having th at photograph appear on th e company’s website, and
that website saying she was endorsing their products constitutes a breach of the Cabinet
Manual. It constitutes a conflict of interest that John Key today says is no problem to
him. Well, I say to him to release that a dvice. Release that advice today, because for
most New Zealanders Judith Collins’ actions are a clear conflict of interest.
It is not as if this visit to the Oravida office in Shanghai is Judith Collins’ only action
in this regard. She also opened the Auck land office of Oravida in 2013. Her husband
16342 General Debate 5 Mar 2014
went on the board in 2012. Oravida is also the organisation that donated over $55,000 to
the National Party in 2011.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It was $55,000. So Judith Collins, knowing all of that,
goes to that office and promotes the products  of that company. That is a conflict of
interest. Judith Collins is not above the rule s. She is not above the law. This National
Government might be arrogant enough to thi nk it is above the rules and above the law,
but it is not. New Zealanders want to know  that when Ministers go overseas, it is
taxpayer money well spent. What they have se en here is a Minister prepared to flout
what a conflict of interest is to most people.
This company is not one that just Judith Collins has a deep involvement in; this
company is also one that reaches far into the National Party. I will table at the end of
this speech further information from the Or avida website that makes clear that when
Oravida sponsored a group of business people from China to come to New Zealand in
2012, they met with Peter Goodfellow, who was identified by Oravida on the website as
the “National Party chairman”, to discus s the exciting opportuni ty of extensively
developing a foundation for bila teral collaborations. That is  Peter Goodfellow, as the
president of the National Party, meeting in that position—not in his role as a
businessman, apparently, but as the presiden t of the National Party—to help extend the
relationship with this company, Oravida. What  I can also tell the House is that Mr
Goodfellow’s company Sanford supplies fish products to Oravida. So we now have a
situation where the president of the Nationa l Party—meeting in that position; giving an
endorsement, effectively, to the relationship between that company and New Zealand—
is also supplying products and benefiting from that.
Here we have a company where a senior Ca binet Minister’s husband is on the board.
He is going about his business as a direct or in a way that will benefit him and will
benefit that company. The Minister goes to China, appears in photographs, has a
statement that she is endorsing this company, and opens its office. We have donations to
the party. The National Party is in donkey deep with its cronies once again here, and
there are questions to answer for Judith Collins and J ohn Key about whether they think
it is acceptable to have this level of conflict of interest.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What about Pansy Wong?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: This is Pansy Wong all over again.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: What a dreadful start to the year it
has been for the beleaguered Labour Oppositio n and its oleaginous leader du jour, Mr
David Cunliffe. No wonder the heads we re down on the Opposition benches. Those
members could not even pretend to be inte rested or supportive as he was putting
questions to the Prime Minister this afte rnoon. This is the “Member for Herne Bay $2.5
Million Do-uppers”, who is trying to pretend to  the nation at large that he is a man of
the people, that he has got the interests of the public at heart, and that he understands the
common man, or whatever the term might be these days. Half of the Labour Opposition
looked to be suffering severe pain while he  was speaking and the other half looked like
possums trapped in the headlights. Most of those members did not want him. You have
got to give them credit for that—at least they understood that. They tried to tell
Labour’s members and they tried to tell th e unions, but those other parties in Labour’s
overall cluster said: “No, we know best, and you have got to have him.”, and he is
proving to be even worse than they feared he would be.
Let us see what that veteran New Zealand Herald columnist John Armstrong, who
has been around for a long time and who knows the scene, had to say today. Under the
headline “Two Cunliffe mea culpas in four days smacks of clumsiness”, John

items.speaker: Armstrong wrote
items.text: “That he cannot seem to  stop his fingers hove ring over the self-
5 Mar 2014 General Debate 16343
destruct button is no surprise  to anyone who has watched him for any length of time.”
What a devastating comment that is from  a man of John Armstrong’s experience. He
goes on to say: “It is a gr eat mystery why someone overl y blessed with essential
political attributes gets it wrong with su ch frequency. Maybe it is overconfidence.
Maybe it is an inability to see the line be tween being bold and be ing foolhardy. He got
away with it when he held lower ranked pos itions in the Labour caucus. The role of
Leader of the Opposition offers no escape from the spotlight.”, and so it goes on. A
devastating critique—devastating because of its unbelievable accuracy.
This is a leader who relies on dodgy CVs, a leader who relies on secret trusts, and a
leader who relies on blatant bribes for voters with promises  that do not stack up and
could not possibly be afforded. He is so desperate to win support from a few of his
caucus that he is promising them a bonus if they would just go forth and multiply. How
ridiculous it is to suggest that the new benc hmark for poverty in this country is just a
little bit more than a backbe nch MP’s salary. Boy, that is going to be a winner on the
hustings this year! It is about as credib le as suggesting that a $2.5 million home in
Herne Bay is just a modest do-upper in middl e New Zealand. Yet it is consistent with
all the other nonsense that has been coming out  of a party that is  hopelessly divided,
hopelessly bereft of sensible or constructive  ideas, and hopelessly out of touch with the
electorate.
The Labour Party hopes to convince New Zeala nders later this year  that it was not
responsible for getting this country into th e recession when it was in Government, and
yet, somehow, it has also got the best policies for continuing to lead us out of it. Well,
as the Prime Minister noted in question tim e today, our economy is the envy of most
other countries and commentators in the developed world. Why is that? Well, the
National-led Government’s programme to bu ild a faster-growing economy, with more
jobs and rising incomes, is being shown to deliver.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Where are the jobs?

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: There are lots of jobs being created in my electorate, and I
invite you to come and see it. In fact, a lo t of the jobs are now in your electorate,
because Haier has just announced 65 new jobs  in Dunedin. Yet your leader, that rather
confused Mr Cunliffe, was opposed to something that has actually turned out to be very
good for your own electorate.
I would like to put on record a few of the contrasts between what we inherited from
the Labour Government and its record and what we have got now. The current account
deficit when National took office after 9 year s of Labour was 9 percent of GDP. Today
the current account deficit is 4.3 percent of  GDP. Net external debt under Labour blew
out to 84 percent of GDP. Today it is down to  71 percent of GDP. It is still too high and
we are getting it down, and we must continue  to do so. Inflation was running at more
than 5 percent under Labour. Today under National it is 1.6 percent. Mortgage interest
rates averaged nearly 11 percent. Today they  average about half that amount. And so it
goes on. These are the important things that  matter to New Zealanders, these are the
things that we can campaign on this year, a nd these are the things that New Zealanders
want us to continue to deliver.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I said that I would table a
document at the end of my speech, so I seek leave to table a document from the Oravida
website—it is not easy to obtain—from J une 2012 about a visit from the Shanghai
municipality to New Zealand—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I think the document has be en described. I suspect it is
actually relatively easy to source, but I am in a very generous mood. I will put the leave.
Leave is sought to table this particular document from th e website of the company. Is
there any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
16344 General Debate 5 Mar 2014
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: We heard earlier this afternoon in question time about
some improvements in the delivery of drug and alcohol treatment to inmates in our
prisons, and that is a good thing. I suspect that it will not be sufficient, but it is a step
forward, and I acknowledge that this Minister of Correctio ns has made some genuine
efforts to improve the situation around impris onment and incarceration. It is too little,
but at least there are some good ideas and some good initiatives being seen.
Sadly, in the overall picture, however, we have a very long  way to go. I believe that
some New Zealanders would be disappointed and surprised, and even ashamed, at some
of the events and some of the conditions that  are observable in some of our prisons. We
have had two recent documents from watc hdogs, independent bodies with no political
axe to grind, that are very clearly and very  graphically outlining some of the appalling
conditions that people are being subject to in our prisons—something that is way below
the mark for a country that prides itself on respect for human rights and the rule of law.
A report from the Human Rights Commission in December, Monitoring Places of
Detention, talked about the dreadful conditions in at least two of our  prisons to which
segregated prisoners are being subjected. It talks about particularly bad living
conditions for segregated inmates at Auck land and Mt Eden prisons. It refers to
accommodation for prisoners currently undergoing periods of segregation as being
“well below standard and could be considered cruel and inhumane for the purpose of the
Convention Against Torture.” I believe that  it would shock and disappoint many New
Zealanders that we are subjecting inmates in  our prisons to conditions that could be
considered cruel and inhuma ne under the Optional Protocol  to the Convention against
Torture. It is simply not good enough, and it is something that we need to pay some real
attention to.
There were general shortcomings found in the whole matter of se gregation in that
document, in that report. We are told that part of the solution is a rebuild of the
maximum security wing at P āremoremo prison, but that will not begin until some time
later this year. I ask the question: when th ere is such a patent need for decent humane
accommodation for these inmates, why has that work at Pāremoremo not been advanced
ahead of the $900 million white elephant currently being constructed at Wiri?
The second document, the second report fr om just a few weeks ago, is a special
investigation into the manage ment of a prisoner by the na me of Arthur Taylor at
Auckland prison. Again, this finds that Mr Taylor was initially put into segregation for a
period of 14 days for the possession of a ce llphone, which, yes, is something he ought
not to have had. That 14-day segregation wa s extended to 8 months. For 8 months this
man was subjected, effectively, to 23-hours- a-day lockdown. He was deprived of
association with, and the company of, othe r inmates. He was deprived of basic
minimum requirements that ought to be provi ded to every inmate. Those findings come
from our own Office of the Ombudsmen, wh ich I would argue is beyond dispute in
terms of its observation. For 8 months the Department of Corrections failed to follow its
own rules. There was a complete breakdown in  its checks and balances. Decisions were
made in advance of information being pres ented. There were process failures, which
have been noted by the ombudsman. There we re failures to pr ovide even minimum
requirements. For many days and, indeed, w eeks at a time this inmate had no access to
exercise in the outside.
This situation needs a response. It is no light matter. I have signed a letter, along with
others, including a QC and barristers, aski ng the Commissioner of Police to consider
whether criminal charges ought to be brought against the management of P āremoremo
prison and, indeed, against th e Chief Executive of the Department of Corrections for
5 Mar 2014 General Debate 16345
their failure in their duty of care to inmates. They are legislatively obliged to ensure that
the inmates in our prisons are treated decently and humanely. According to the evidence
of the ombudsman and the Hu man Rights Commission, they fa iled in their duty of care
in ways that could well put them in contra vention of our Crimes of Torture Act. We
have asked the police to investigate that. We need to do a great deal better in our
prisons. It is not good enough, an d we look to a better time  with a more progressive
Government. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Fifty years ago, in 1963, in a small town in
Te Aroha in the North Island one David Ri chard Cunliffe was being born. Sitting on
one side of the bed was the good fairy. The good fairy blessed David Richard Cunliffe
with charm, intelligence, and good looks—a leader in the making. Unfortunately, sitting
on the other side of the bed wa s the bad fairy, who made hi m out to be the plonker that
he is today. The other side of the House knows that the bad fairy won out on that day,
because it is having such a tough time doing any good work and trying to get up in the
polls.
Across the House I see Grant Robertson smiling. He is smiling because he knows
that he is next in line. He is next in line. Chris Hipkins is smiling, too, I can see—sitting
on the other side of the Leader of the Opposition’s seat—because Chris Hipkins knows
that he was right. Chris Hipkins  knows that when he said that David Cunliffe could not
be trusted, he was absolutely right. The Labou r Party has had a heck of a year. It is
going backwards, it is not going forwards, and it knows that it is not going well.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You got here because of Pansy.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: During question time, Annette King, who is calling out right
now—also Parliament’s most famous landla dy, superannuitant, and someone who has
been here longer than I have  been alive—called out “Shambles.” She used the word
“shambles”. She used the word “shambles”. I want to expand on that. I want to use the
term coined by the British political scene’s most famous spin doctor, Malcolm Tucker.
He would call what the Labour Party is goi ng through an omnishambles. It is going
through an omnishambles right now—an omnish ambles where it just  cannot get things
right.
Its leader is tricky. It s leader was blessed by the bad fairy. Donations are being kept
secret, when those members are the ones who try to say that donations need to be
brought out into the op en. Leaked emails are coming out of the Labour Party left, right,
and centre. Poor old Clare Curran got blamed for it, then a staff member got blamed for
